Name: Sawmill Creek Camp
Summary: The main North Fork campground, with creek-side sites under big cedars and the valley's trailheads within walking distance.
Description:
Sites sit in two loops along the creek. The lower loop is closest to the water and the loudest after rain. The upper loop is quieter and gets morning sun.

There is a tap at each loop, flush toilets, and a bear-proof food locker at every site. Firewood is sold at the host site in the evening.

Book well ahead for July and August weekends.

Name: Lookout Road Camp
Summary: A small, high camp at the gate on Lookout Road, used as a base for the lookout and the traverse.
Description:
Eight walk-in sites in a meadow beside the gate. Water is from the stream and must be treated. There is one pit toilet and no host.

The camp is cold at night even in August. It is the natural start for the traverse and the lookout.

First come, first served. It rarely fills except on long weekends.

Name: Saddle Pass Camp
Summary: An alpine campground at the pass with the summit, the larches, and the meadows all starting from your tent.
Description:
The camp sits on the lee side of the pass in stunted fir. Sites are small and close together, and the wind finds all of them.

There is a tap, two pit toilets, and a cooking shelter with a wood stove. Fires are not allowed outside the shelter.

The larch season books out months ahead. The rest of the summer is easier.

Name: Cirque Creek Camp
Summary: A free, basic camp at the Cirque Creek bridge for early starts into the cirque.
Description:
Six cleared sites in the trees by the bridge, with a pit toilet and a food cache. Water is from the creek.

The camp is used mostly by parties heading into the cirque at first light. It is quiet, dark, and cold.

No dogs, to match the cirque trail.

Name: Reservoir Beach Camp
Summary: The big family campground on the upper reservoir, with a beach, a boat launch, and hot showers.
Description:
Forty-two drive-in sites in four loops above a sandy beach. The lakeside loop is the most popular and the most expensive.

Showers, flush toilets, a dish station, and a small shop at the host site. Canoes can be rented at the launch.

Quiet hours are enforced from ten. This is a family campground and it feels like one.

Name: Bluff Camp
Summary: A walk-in camp below the Basin Bluffs, used on the two-day link from the coast.
Description:
Ten walk-in sites on a bench below the bluffs, a ten-minute carry from the Bluff Road trailhead. There is a tap, a pit toilet, and a shared fire ring.

The camp faces south and is warm in spring and autumn. It is the overnight stop for the Bluff to Basin Link.

Pay at the self-registration post.

Name: Cove Lane Camp
Summary: A sheltered coastal campground in the trees above Smugglers Cove, open all year.
Description:
Eighteen sites in a sheltered hollow behind the bluffs. The trees keep the wind off and the cove is a ten-minute walk.

Flush toilets, a tap, and a covered cooking area. No showers.

Open all year. Winter is quiet and the storms are worth seeing from the bluffs.

Name: Estuary Camp
Summary: A simple campground beside the estuary, popular with birdwatchers at dawn.
Description:
Twelve sites on short grass beside the estuary road. Flat, open, and close to the boardwalk and the hides.

A tap and two pit toilets. There is no shade and no shelter from the wind.

First come, first served, and rarely full outside the autumn migration.
